newsitem.title: UK: Central bank fears hobbled 1996 gold market says report.
newsitem.headline: Central bank fears hobbled 1996 gold market says report.

text.p: Fear of gold sales by central banks and other institutions dominated gold last year and capped prices as market sentiment tottered, Gold Fields Mineral Services Ltd. said in its annual report Wednesday.

Gold fabrication demand reached a new high as total consumption of the metal reached 3,490 metric tons, outrunning supply by 163 tons, according to the report, compiled before news that Bre-X Minerals Ltd.'s Busang find in Indonesia, touted as the world's potentially biggest gold discovery, was a sham.

But total consumption was still 139 tons lower than 1995's level, and investors who shied away from gold sold enough of their hoardings to limit the imbalance, the market analyst firm said in its Gold 1997 report.
Supplies of newly mined gold rose to 2,346 tons from 2,269 in 1995, although South Africa mined less than 500 tons for the first time in a single year since 1956. Its output was 496 tons.

The net result of weak sentiment and investor interest against only a marginal increases in fabrication demand and slightly higher supply was a 1 percent rise in the average gold price to $387.87 per ounce vs. $384.05 in 1995.
But the report noted that the sustained rise in the value of the dollar meant that gold prices in many other currencies were substantial higher from a year earlier.

"The price weakness since the last quarter of 1996 has been to a large extent the result of poor sentiment stemming above all from fears about the future impact of the official sector on the gold market," said Gold Fields' Chief Executive Stewart Murray.
The physical demand, he said, supported gold prices around $340, but "only time will tell whether this floor can become a foundation for the kind of rally seen in the second quarter of 1993."
The most important influence on the price was the role of the official gold holders, it said.

More than 500 tons of gold were sold by the Belgian and Dutch central banks between them in the first and fourth quarters of the year, and 14 other central banks added 88 tons of gold sales during the year.

More significant still was the perception that further official sales were likely from the International Monetary Fund, the Swiss National Bank and any one of several European central banks on the way to European Monetary Union.
